item.title: Formed for solidarity
item.description: Last summer my team at Episcopal Divinity School hosted a screening of the 1999 documentary Here Am I, Send Me: The Journey of Jonathan Daniels. Daniels, a White man from New Hampshire and a student at EDS (then called Episcopal Theological School), was killed in 1965 while volunteering with the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee to register Black voters in Lowndes County, Alabama.

item.title: February 18 Ash Wednesday Joel 2 1 2 12 17 Psalm 51 1 17 2 Corinthians 5 20b 6 10 nbsp Matthew 6 1 6 16 21
item.description: Can I ask a simple question? I don’t mean to be rude or argumentative. In fact, this year for Lent I am giving up rude and argumentative, along with their many behavioral and spiritual cognates: pride, presumption, priggishness, puffery. Much in the same way as, last year, I gave up curmudgeonliness and judgmentalism, though admittedly without either immediate or protracted success.

item.title: As Walk for Peace reaches DC Buddhist monks share interfaith message with thousands
item.description: Thousands of onlookers gathered at Washington National Cathedral on Tuesday to see and hear from the Buddhist monks who have completed a 108-day, 2,300-mile walking journey from Texas to the nation’s capital. Surrounded by leaders from several faith traditions, including Washington Episcopal Bishop Mariann Budde, who began the gathering with a peace prayer from St. Francis, the monks talked about how the practice of compassion can transcend religious differences.

item.title: Danced religion at halftime
item.description: Bad Bunny swerved, subverting everyone’s expectations of a political statement. Since it was announced in September that Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio (Bad Bunny) would be the halftime performer for Super Bowl LX, the question being asked was, “What political statement will Bad Bunny make?”

item.title: February 22 Lent 1A Matthew 4 1 11
item.description: A doctor buddy of mine, who is no biblical literalist, is nonetheless convinced that the story of Jesus in the wilderness is both factual and true. His assumption is that this wilderness is the same wilderness Jesus traversed in search of John, full of the selfsame angels and beasts and temptations, only unseen until after he found his cousin and was baptized by him.
